The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(N=2100\). For a prime \(p\) and integer \(r\ge 1\), track how many entries on the board are divisible by \(p^r\).

If \(a,b\) are replaced by \(\gcd(a,b),\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\), then for each prime \(p\) the two \(p\)-adic valuations are replaced by their minimum and maximum. Thus the number of entries divisible by \(p^r\) is invariant. Initially this number is

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^r}\right\rfloor.
\]

When Mark stops, no move changes the board. For two positive integers \(a,b\), replacing them by \(\gcd(a,b),\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\) leaves the pair unchanged exactly when one divides the other. Hence the final entries form a chain under divisibility.

Order the final entries as

\[
x_1\mid x_2\mid \cdots \mid x_{2100}.
\]

This is also numerical order. For a fixed \(p,r\), the entries divisible by \(p^r\) form a suffix of this chain. The \(2026\)th smallest entry is \(x_{2026}\), the first of the last

\[
2100-2026+1=75
\]

entries. Therefore \(p^r\mid x_{2026}\) if and only if at least \(75\) final entries are divisible by \(p^r\), i.e.

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^r}\right\rfloor\ge 75.
\]

Since \(2100=75\cdot 28\), this is equivalent to

\[
p^r\le 28.
\]

So the exponent of \(p\) in \(x_{2026}\) is the largest \(r\) with \(p^r\le 28\).

Thus:

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2(x_{2026})&=4 &&(2^4=16\le 28<32),\\
v_3(x_{2026})&=3 &&(3^3=27\le 28<81),\\
v_5(x_{2026})&=2 &&(5^2=25\le 28<125),\\
v_p(x_{2026})&=1 &&\text{for }p=7,11,13,17,19,23.
\end{aligned}
\]

All other primes have exponent \(0\). Therefore the number of positive divisors of \(x_{2026}\) is

\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2^6
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
